Part 1: The Data (2 points)¶

We will be exploring a data set on Women's March Madness (Basketball). This adapted data set contains historical records of every NCAA Division I Women’s Basketball Tournament appearance since the tournament began in 1982 up until 2018. Sourced from official NCAA records, the adapted data set captures tournament results across more than four decades of collegiate women’s basketball. All data is sourced from the NCAA and contains the data behind the story "The Rise and Fall Of Women’s NCAA Tournament Dynasties."

The data set can be read in from the following url: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diverse-data-hub/diversedata/refs/heads/main/data-clean/womensmarchmadness.csv

To help you with the analysis, here is a table of descriptions of each of the variables present in the model.

Variable Description
year Year
school School Name
seed Seed. The 0 seeding designation in 1983 notes the eight teams that played an opening-round game to become the No. 8 seed in each region.
conference Conference
conf_wins Conference Wins
conf_losses Conference Losses
conf_wins_pct Conference Win Percentage
conf_rank Place in Conference
division Conference Division
reg_wins Regional Wins
reg_losses Regional Losses
reg_wins_pct Regional Win Percentage
bid Whether the school qualified with an automatic bid (by winning its conference or conference tournament) or an at-large bid. [‘at-large’, ‘auto’]
first_game_at_home Whether the school played its first-round tournament games on its home court. [‘Y’, ‘N’]
tourney_wins Tourney Wins
tourney_losses Tourney Losses
tourney_finish Ordered categories: [‘opening_round_loss’ < ‘first_round_loss’ < ‘second_round_loss’ < ‘top_16_loss’ < ‘top_8_loss’ < ‘top_4_loss’ < ‘top_2_loss’ < ‘champ’]
total_wins Total Wins
total_losses Total Losses
total_wins_pct Total Win Percentage

Part 5: Analysis (34 points)¶

In this section, you will describe your data analysis and perform it.

Task 5.1 Plan out your analysis (10 points)¶

Propose a method that was covered in class that would be appropriate to use to answer your research question. You only need to build one model with one set of predictors in this section. Write a paragraph that explains the choice of method, and be sure to answer the following questions:

  • What method do you plan to use?
  • Why is this method appropriate?
  • What are the potential limitations or weaknesses of the method selected?
  • How are you going to process the data to apply the model? For example: Are you splitting the data? How? How many splits? What proportions will you use for the splits? At what stage will you split? Will there be a validation set? Will you use cross validation?
  • How will you assess the performance of the model? Explain why the performance metric(s) chosen are appropriate.

You answer should be around 250 words or less.

To answer my research question of whether conference win percentage and regional win percentage can indicate if a school played its first‑round tournament game at home—I plan to use k‑nearest neighbours classification. This method is appropriate because my outcome variable, first_game_at_home, is binary (“Y” or “N”), and KNN is designed to classify observations into categories based on similarity in predictor space. Since my predictors (conference win percentage and regional win percentage) are numeric and on comparable scales, they are well‑suited for distance‑based methods like KNN. Another advantage is that KNN makes no assumptions about linearity, which is useful if the relationship between win percentages and home‑court status is nonlinear.

However, KNN has limitations. It can perform poorly with very small datasets, and my dataset contains only 20 observations. Because KNN relies on distances, it is also sensitive to outliers and requires predictors to be standardized. Additionally, KNN can overfit if k is too small or underfit if k is too large, so tuning is important.

To apply the model, I will split the data into training and testing sets using a 75/25 split, performed before any preprocessing to avoid data leakage. I will use cross‑validation on the training set to choose the best value of k. The test set will be used only for final evaluation. I will assess model performance using accuracy, which is an appropriate metrics for binary classification.

Task 5.2 Perform the Analysis (20 points)¶

  • Perform the proposed analysis.
  • Be sure to comment your code throughout so that it is easy to follow.

You may add more code cells if needed.

In [69]:
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

#split the dataset
basketball_split <- initial_split(woman_basketball_selected, prop = 0.75, strata = first_game_at_home) #75:25 proportion
basketball_train <- training(basketball_split)
basketball_test <- testing(basketball_split) |>
mutate(first_game_at_home = as_factor(first_game_at_home))  
#create the recipe and scale the data
basketball_recipe <- recipe(first_game_at_home ~ conf_wins_pct + reg_wins_pct, data = basketball_train) |>
  step_scale(all_predictors()) |>
  step_center(all_predictors())
#create the model for the training set
knn_spec <- nearest_neighbor(weight_func = "rectangular", neighbors = tune()) |>
  set_engine("kknn") |>
  set_mode("classification")
#build the workflow
knn_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(basketball_recipe) |>
  add_model(knn_spec) |>
  fit(data = basketball_train)
#set up cross-validation
basketball_vfold <- vfold_cv(basketball_train, v = 5, strata = first_game_at_home) #5 folds for training set
#tune k using cross-validation
k_grid <- tibble(neighbors = seq(from = 1, to = 25, by = 2)) 
knn_tuned <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(basketball_recipe) |>
  add_model(knn_spec) |>
  tune_grid(resamples = basketball_vfold, grid = k_grid)|>
  collect_metrics()
#choose the best k
accuracies <- knn_tuned |>
  filter(.metric == "accuracy") #using the "accuracy" metrics
best_k <- accuracies |> 
arrange(desc(mean)) |> #finding k with the smallest RMSE
head(1) |>
pull(neighbors)
#retrain the K-NN model for train set
basketball_recipe <- recipe(first_game_at_home ~ conf_wins_pct + reg_wins_pct, data = basketball_train) |>
  step_scale(all_predictors()) |>
  step_center(all_predictors())
knn_spec <- nearest_neighbor(weight_func = "rectangular", neighbors = best_k) |> #using the best k as the number of neighbors
  set_engine("kknn") |>
  set_mode("classification")
knn_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(basketball_recipe) |>
  add_model(knn_spec) |>
  fit(data = basketball_train)
#evaluate on the test set using accuracy
basketball_test_predictions <- predict(knn_fit, basketball_test) |>
  bind_cols(basketball_test)
basketball_test_predictions |>
  mutate(.pred_class = factor(.pred_class, levels = levels(first_game_at_home))) |> #because "truth" and "estimate" are not in the same order - `truth`: Y and N, and estimate`: N and Y, so I make them in the same order 
  accuracy(truth = first_game_at_home, estimate = .pred_class)
basketball_test_predictions

Task 5.3 Create a Visualization or Table of the Results of your Analysis (4 points)¶

  • Create a visualization or table that is relevant to the results of your analysis (comment your code throughout so that it is easy to follow).
  • Describe what this visualization or table is showing, and why it is important to the analysis (approx 150 words or less).

This plot displays the mean cross‑validated accuracy for each tested value of k in the k‑nearest neighbours model. Each point represents the model’s performance for a specific number of neighbours, and the connecting line highlights the overall trend. In this graph, accuracy increases quickly at small k values, then levels off and fluctuates slightly as k becomes larger. It shows that very small k tends to overfit, while very large k can underfit. The peak region of the curve (k = 23) indicates the k values that balance these forces most effectively. This visualization is important because it provides a transparent justification for selecting the final k used in my model. It shows that the chosen k was not arbitrary but based on systematic evaluation of predictive performance across multiple candidate values.

In [72]:
accuracy_vs_k <- ggplot(accuracies, aes(x = neighbors, y = mean)) +
  geom_point() + #each point represents a single performance done by each k
  geom_line() + #line graph illustrates the trend of change in accuracy throughout the change in k 
  labs(x = "Neighbors (k)", y = "Accuracy Estimate") + #the relationship between k and accuracy
  theme(text = element_text(size = 12))

Part 6: Discuss your Results (10 points)¶

In this section, you will discuss some interesting findings from your analysis in Part 5

Task 6.1: Discuss your findings (10 points)¶

In 1 to 2 paragraphs (approx. 300 words or less):

  • Summarize what you found from the analysis in Part 5, in relation to your research question of interest.
  • The data science workflow is an iterative process. Discuss if at any point you had to adjust your analysis plan based on the results.
  • Discuss whether this is what you expected, or if anything was surprising.
  • Discuss the impact of the results, and what future questions this could lead to.

My analysis shows that conference win percentage and regular‑season win percentage carry some predictive signal about whether a school hosted its first‑round tournament game, but the relationship is not very strong. After tuning the k‑nearest neighbours model, accuracy on the test set suggests that teams with stronger performance during the season are more likely to play at home, but the model still makes some errors. This implies that while win percentages matter, they are not the only—or even the dominant—factors determining home‑court assignment. The workflow required adjustment when tuning revealed that accuracy did not improve consistently with larger k values. This led to refining the grid of k values and re‑running cross‑validation to ensure the chosen k was stable. It was also necessary to correct factor‑level mismatches and ensure the train/test split remained consistent, which reflects the iterative nature of data science, which is that each step can reveal issues that require revisiting earlier decisions.

The results were partly expected. Better teams tend to have advantages, but the relatively modest accuracy was surprising, showing that performance alone cannot reliably indicate home‑court status. This give some hints to future questions: Would adding variables like team ranking or tournament region improve predictive power? Could a logistic regression capture nonlinear patterns that kNN misses? Exploring these directions could deepen understanding of how tournament logistics and competitive strength interact.
